tweets.text: Using Gemini 4 makes you realize how many other models must be distilling Claude/GPT (or using a similar training pipeline). It feels quite different than other models.

I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. 

On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base.

Here is a fun example:  "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end"

I suspect the vast majority of these are nitpicks, so I wouldn't assume that they overturn results and papers. They don't fall into the normal corrections process, making it hard to understand how to handle them well within the constraints of academic publishing.

GPT-6 Pro finds supposed errors in academic papers all the time, just as part of other work. Confirming the errors & learning their importance would still take a lot of time today, but it will get faster. We don't have the right mechanisms in place to deal a flood of corrections.

As long as LLMs continue to be unreasonably good at everything, companies will figure out a way to muddle along. But they are often struggling with managing organization change, and frequent mandatory model switches (looking at you, Google) and other changes are hard for them.

I spoke to some annoyed leaders at big firms who were still big on GPTs as of last month, before GPTs were sunsetted. Yes, GPTs outlived their usefulness. But large organizations have complex planning & all the Labs (not just OpenAI) keep making sudden changes that confuse them.

The most advanced models are also more creative and more insightful and better at nuance and better at qualitative data and more capable of producing things of beauty and more helpful to people who need help of all kinds. (And, yes, more capable of bad stuff too, of course)

Not to get too annoying about it but its worth noting that many of the 5,000 people at the labs with access to advanced model still haven't used them to their full extent: its all cybersecurity &  math & AI R&D.
